stimulus.text:
“There is no Declaration of Rights; and the Laws of the general Government being paramount to the Laws & Constitution of the several States, the Declarations of Rights in the separate States are no Security. . . . In the House of Representatives there is not the Substance, but the Shadow only of Representation; which can never produce proper Information in the Legislature, or inspire Confidence in the people. . . . The Judiciary of the United States is so constructed & extended, as to absorb & destroy the Judiciarys of the several States. . . . There is no Declaration of any kind for preserving the Liberty of the Press, the Tryal by jury in civil Causes; nor against the Danger of standing Armies in time of Peace.”

—George Mason, Objections to the Constitution of Government formed by the Convention, September 1787
stimulus.source_note: George Mason, Objections to the Constitution of Government formed by the Convention, September 1787. Public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.8 The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification, C. Federalists, Anti-Federalists, and the Adoption of the Bill of Rights

primary_sources: George Mason, Objections to the Constitution of Government formed by the Convention (September 1787)

stem: According to Mason, what is missing first and foremost from the Constitution?

options.text: A president with power to enforce the laws
options.misconception: The passage never says the presidency is missing; Mason's first objection is a declaration of rights.

options.text: A Senate with equal representation for each state
options.misconception: The Senate's equal representation was in the Constitution; Mason objects to the House, not the Senate's design.

options.text: A ban on standing armies in time of peace
options.misconception: Mason lists standing armies last among his objections, not first; the declaration of rights opens the list.

rationales.C: Mason's objections open with the words themselves: There is no Declaration of Rights.
rationales.A: The presidency is not in the passage; the first objection is the missing declaration of rights.
rationales.B: Background: equal representation in the Senate was part of the Constitution, and Mason's complaint is about the House.
rationales.D: Standing armies appear near the end of the list, not at its head.
rationales.general:
1. Read the first words of the objections: There is no Declaration of Rights.
2. Mason puts that objection first, before the House, the judiciary, and the press.
3. Background: the missing bill of rights became the Anti-Federalists' central demand in ratification.
4. So the answer is the first item on Mason's own list.
Remember: when a writer lists objections, the first one is the one he leads with.
